messages.content:
I'll approach this from basic physics principles. In a time-of-flight mass spectrometer, ions are accelerated by an electric field and then travel through a field-free region before reaching the detector. The key physics principles involve the conservation of energy.

When an ion with charge q is accelerated through a potential difference V, it gains kinetic energy:

Potential energy = q·V
Kinetic energy = (1/2)·m·v²

By the conservation of energy: q·V = (1/2)·m·v²

Solving for velocity: v = √(2·q·V/m)

From this equation, we can see that the velocity (v) is inversely proportional to the square root of the mass (m), since v ∝ 1/√m.

This means that lighter ions will travel faster than heavier ions after being accelerated through the same potential difference.
